transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-21
Start: 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~30 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Cole (Recruiter), Dr. Lila Nguyen (Hiring Manager), Kai Chen (Candidate)

Summary:
Quick phone screen for Staff/Principal-ish inference engineer. Focus on candidate background in production inference, quantization experience, debugging latency regressions and kernel-level profiling. Recruiter-led intro, then technical lead asked clarifying questions. Candidate to receive a short take-home design prompt.

Topics:
- Candidate background and current role
- Experience with model serving, quantization, NVidia/TensorRT or ONNX stack
- Debugging/repro steps for latency spikes
- Availability and timeline

Action items (recap): send design prompt; confirm panel; candidate to complete take-home

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ethan: Hey Kai, this is Ethan from Redwood, thanks for taking the time. You can hear me ok?
[00:06] Kai: Yeah, loud and clear, thanks Ethan. Appreciate it.
[00:09] Ethan: Quick call, about half an hour. I'll do a short recruiter intro then Lila will do some technical questions, cool?
[00:15] Kai: Sounds good.
[00:18] Ethan: Awesome. So very top-line, Redwood Inference builds inference infra and we are hiring for someone to help with our serving runtime and performance work. Lila is the hiring manager, she'll dive deeper. For context, can you give us a one-minute summary of your current role and what you've been owning?
[00:33] Kai: Sure. Currently I'm at Nimbus Labs, I'm senior SRE-ish on the ML infra team, mainly responsible for the production stack that serves recommendation and search models. I own the inference platform components — autoscaling, model packaging, and a bunch of perf work. Recently I led a quantization project to move some models from FP32 to int8 using ONNX runtime and a TensorRT path. We got a 3x reduction in p99 latency on a couple of endpoints after caching and re-tuning the kernels.
[01:02] Lila: 3x p99 is solid, curious — when you say re-tuning kernels, do you mean you changed TensorRT heuristics or you wrote custom fused kernels?
[01:10] Kai: Mostly heuristics and some custom casting paths. We wrote a small shim in CUDA to handle mixed-precision casting for layer norms that was causing numeric blow up. Mostly engineering tradeoffs — we also had to adjust sequence-length padding since the batching semantics were hurting throughput.
[01:27] Lila: Nice. Did you use any perf tools — nsight, perf, or something custom to pinpoint the hot spots?
[01:32] Kai: We used Nsight for kernel hotspots, and a custom sampling-based tracer we built that annotates requests with KV cache hits/misses. The tracer has some false positives — it misattributed cold-starts a few times — but it was good enough to find the bad kernels.
[01:46] Ethan: Quick recruiter question — what's your target timeline? Are you actively interviewing?
[01:50] Kai: I'm open now, would like to move in the next 4-8 weeks.
[01:55] Ethan: Got it. Compensation expectations? (brief)
[01:57] Kai: Open to discussion, nothing fixed — more focused on impact and team fit.
[02:03] Lila: Back to technical — have you had to support both on-prem and cloud deployment mixes? Any experience with VPC/private deployments or customers that required air-gapped inference?
[02:12] Kai: Yes, we had an enterprise customer that required a private deployment. We packaged the runtime into an air-gapped installer and used their HSM for keys. Biggest pain was telemetry — had to write a proxy that buffers traces and emits only redacted summaries over a controlled egress.
[02:29] Lila: That aligns with some of our Private work. How comfortable are you with writing production-grade telemetry and tracing hooks?
[02:36] Kai: Comfortable. I've pushed sampling-based traces that annotate token-level latencies. We faced a challenge where sampling overhead changed tail latency; we solved it by moving sampling to an out-of-band sidecar and only attaching metadata to the request path.
[02:50] Lila: Makes sense. Have you worked on model fallback or graceful degradation strategies when capacity is constrained?
[02:57] Kai: Yeah, we implemented a tiered routing policy — smaller, quantized variants for non-critical traffic, with a fallback to CPU cached responses for extremely low-latency callbacks. It was a bit ugly but worked.
[03:12] Ethan: Speaker background — any open-source contributions we should see?
[03:16] Kai: I have a repo with some inference utilities and a small transformer-optimized kernel. I can share links.
[03:21] Lila: Please do. Also, can you talk through a time you debugged a sudden p99 spike in production? Step-by-step?
[03:29] Kai: Sure — we saw a 2.5x p99 increase during a canary. First I pulled traces to see which model and route was affected, then we checked kernel-level metrics — temperature, memcopy times, occupancy. We noticed that a new quantization profile for a batch path increased memcpy overhead because of an unexpected padding pattern. Rolling back that quantization reduced p99 but didn't fix the root cause; we then instrumented per-token queuing times and found that a bad batching heuristic at the router side increased queue delays for longer sequences. We changed the batch heuristic to be sequence-length aware and introduced a cap on max-batch-delay; that brought p99 down.
[04:06] Lila: Good detail — did you have unit tests or synthetic load that reproduced the issue?
[04:11] Kai: We were able to reproduce with a synthetic harness that mimicked sequence-length distribution and cold-starts; it required a particular ordering of small and large sequences to hit the bug, which is why it escaped canary initially.
[04:23] Ethan: Any particular languages and frameworks you prefer — C++ for kernels, Python for orchestration?
[04:29] Kai: C++/CUDA for kernels; Rust for a few newer services; Python for orchestration and scripts.
[04:34] Lila: Rust — nice. Are you comfortable reading CUDA assembly / PTX when debugging perf?
[04:40] Kai: I'm not writing PTX daily but I can read it and understand the implications. I have used Nsight to inspect SASS a few times.
[04:48] Lila: We sometimes need folks to sketch a design quickly. On a 5–10 minute whiteboard, how would you design a low-latency prefix cache for autoregressive models to reduce repeated KV cache recompute across requests?
[04:58] Kai: Off the top — I'd do a sharded prefix store per-GPU with LRU eviction, keys are (model, prefix-hash, sequence-length-range). For each incoming request, first check local prefix store; if miss, compute partial KV, store and replicate lightweight metadata to a global index. Need to guard against cache pollution so use an admission policy based on observed reuse frequency. Also consider async warming for expected hot prefixes.
[05:25] Lila: Follow-up — how would you serialize the KV cache efficiently and avoid copy overheads?
[05:30] Kai: Memory map pinned pages, use zero-copy transfers where possible; for moving across GPUs within a node use NVLink peer-to-peer, and when crossing hosts use RDMA or a blob-store with pre-shared segments. Also compress with quantized deltas when acceptable.
[05:47] Ethan: We're roughly halfway -- quick logistics: are you open to a take-home design prompt and then a loop if that looks good?
[05:54] Kai: Yes.
[05:56] Ethan: Great. Lila, any closing technical Qs?
[05:59] Lila: A few quick ones — how do you evaluate numeric regressions after quantization? Tolerances?
[06:04] Kai: We use a battery of unit tests: per-output L2/Linf checks, plus downstream metric checks on a holdout set. We also run AB tests with shadow traffic. Tolerances depend on model and task — for ranking a small L2 loss might be acceptable if downstream recall is stable.
[06:20] Lila: Have you owned rollout automation for model variants? Canary, A/B, ring-based?
[06:25] Kai: Yes, ring-based for infra-sensitive customers and canary for open traffic. We automated rollback triggers based on error rates and latency SLOs.
[06:34] Lila: Any experience with KMS/HSM integrations for model keys or telemetry redaction?
[06:38] Kai: Yes, we integrated HashiCorp Vault + AWS KMS for secret handling; in air-gapped env we used HSM provided by the customer.
[06:44] Ethan: Ok logistics — what's your availability for next week for a longer loop?
[06:48] Kai: Evenings are tough, but I can do afternoons PST Tue–Thu.
[06:53] Ethan: We'll try to schedule. A couple of candid notes: we might ask you to do a brief whiteboard during the loop and a more detailed take-home. Does that work?
[07:02] Kai: Yep.
[07:03] Lila: One last question about scale — what size of models have you served (parameters/sequence lengths) and what GPUs?
[07:09] Kai: We serve models in the 1B–7B range primarily, some 13B in off-peak, sequence lengths up to 2k. Hardware mostly A100 and a small fleet of T4s for lower-tier traffic.
[07:24] Lila: Have you done any quantization for 13B — anything special?
[07:28] Kai: For larger models we used mixed schemes: activation quantization to 8-bit with FP16 kernels for matrix multiplies, plus per-channel scales. We had to redesign the optimizer to avoid divergence during fine-tuning.
[07:41] Ethan: Cool. A few quick clarifying things I'll capture as action items. Also please send us your GitHub link and a resume PDF if not already in the system.
[07:50] Kai: Sent resume during application but I'll share Github now.
[07:55] Lila: Ty. Any final q's from you Kai?
[07:58] Kai: Just curious about interview loop composition — is it mostly infra/serving or mixed with infra + research?
[08:05] Lila: Primarily infra and serving with one cross-functional systems interview.
[08:10] Kai: Great.
[08:12] Ethan: Alright we'll follow up with the prompt and panel times. Thanks for your time.
[08:17] Kai: Thanks everyone.

(brief pause)

[15:02] Notes added after call by Ethan: candidate seems strong on practical infra, quantization + debugging experience. Recommended move to take-home design. Candidate available for panel in two weeks.

End of transcript.
